paras: The lynching of William Waters, also reported as William Walters, took place near Mayview, Lafayette County, Missouri, on August 29, 1890, when a crowd hanged a Black youth accused of murdering E. F. Parker, a Mayview merchant, that morning. Seized within hours, Waters was said by his captors to have confessed under a noose and was hanged that night after they hid him from county officers. Wire dispatches presented the case as a murder and lynching completed in one day, and a report on his funeral described indignation among Black residents of the county.

Mayview was a village on the Chicago and Alton railroad about ten miles south of Lexington. Parker, a widower of about 55, kept a store there and slept in a room behind it, while Waters, whose parents lived in Lexington, worked on the farm of Henry C. Shier (also spelled Sheil and Shider) about three miles away.

Parker was found dead behind his counter early on Friday, August 29 with his head nearly severed. According to the Lexington Intelligencer, two Black brothers, Alex and William Dyer, said they had seen a Black man run from the store and Waters inside it with Parker before daylight. A party of men caught Waters on the road; he denied the killing, but they pointed to blood on his clothes and found goods from the store in Shier's barn.

The party then put a halter over his head and swung him up to a barnyard limb, which broke, and as a second noose was readied he cried out that he had killed Parker and led them to a corn knife. Hearing that officers were waiting at Mayview, half the party told them Waters had escaped, while the rest held him bound in nearby woods. After dark, when the officers were believed gone, a large crowd hanged him from a bracket on a telegraph pole and tied the rope to a fence. The body hung until Saturday afternoon, when his mother, Mary Waters, cut it down; he was buried Sunday in the Black cemetery north of Lexington.

A Lexington dispatch of September 2 described a large funeral at the home of Henry Waters, where mourners openly expressed indignation at the hanging. It reported that Black residents of the county were "murmuring," that a "race outbreak" was feared, and that mourners held that a white man would have been left to the law. Mary Waters told the Intelligencer that her son was seventeen years and seven months old and that a trial would have shown someone else was implicated. No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Two wire versions datelined Lexington ran widely on August 30. One relayed Dr. McDonald's report that Constable Thomas Chinn had arrested "William Walters" and that a mob hanged him from a tree. The other had Parker killed with a hatchet and the captured man "given five minutes to pray and then strung up"; the Richmond Times printed his name as "Wm. Walton."

Headlines presented the hanging as prompt punishment: "Swift Justice" in Richmond, "Speedy Retribution" in Los Angeles, "Quick Work" in Fort Worth. The St. Paul Daily Globe added that "a Trial Was Considered Unnecessary," the Omaha Daily Bee called Waters "A Black Fiend," and the Indianapolis Journal stressed "a Negro" and "a White Man's Head."

The Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, whose reporter rode to Mayview with the deputies and coroner, headed its story "Quickly Avenged by Judge Lynch." The Intelligencer's September 6 account, "Two Foul Murders!," paired the case with a same-day killing at Higginsville and called Parker's murder "quickly avenged." It relied on what the captors related and called Waters "the wretch," though it also printed his mother's doubts at length.

Dispatches citing Dr. McDonald said a constable arrested Waters and a mob took him from the officer, while the Intelligencer said a citizens' party captured him and hid him from officers. Accounts also differ on the weapon (hatchet, cleaver or corn knife) and on the gallows (a tree in the wires, a telegraph pole in the Intelligencer). The Intelligencer is local, later and most detailed, but its version of the capture and confession came from the captors themselves.

reader.title: Lynching of William Waters
bases: A crowd seized a Black youth accused of murder, hid him from officers and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A25, A26); wires call it a lynching by a mob (A1, A4).

Waters was hanged without trial by a 'large crowd' of which 'half a-dozen or more men' pulled the rope (A26), in retribution for the murder he was accused of (A1, A25); headlines framed it as 'Swift Justice' (A6).
Independent wire dispatches (A1, A8), a Sedalia reporter at the scene (A19), the local Intelligencer (A25, A26) and a funeral report (A20) agree that Waters was hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: Sedalia reporter

accounts.label: Lexington Intelligencer (captors' account)
accounts.gist: A citizens' party caught Waters on the road, half-hanged him until he confessed, hid him from officers in woods and after dark a large crowd hanged him from a telegraph pole.

accounts.label: Mother and mourners
accounts.gist: Mary Waters believed a trial would have shown others implicated; mourners said a white man would have had the law's course.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Swift Justice', 'Speedy Retribution', 'Quick Work', 'A Mob Avenges a Murder' present the hanging as deserved punishment.
St. Paul Globe: 'a Trial Was Considered Unnecessary'; Omaha Bee: 'A Black Fiend lynched'; Indianapolis Journal stresses 'a Negro' and 'a White Man's Head'.
Lexington Intelligencer calls the murder 'quickly avenged' and Waters 'the wretch' but prints the mother's doubts sympathetically.
Beatrice Daily Express funeral report relays Black residents' indignation and fear of a race outbreak.
